title: Cyclone Arnab hit India in October: the Bay of Bengal has a second storm season
body: On 28 October 2026 Cyclone Arnab, with winds of 115 to 125 km/h gusting to 140, came ashore near Kakinada on India’s east coast, the India Meteorological Department said, as [All India Radio reported](https://newsonair.gov.in/cyclone-arnab-makes-landfall-along-andhra-pradesh-and-yanam-coasts-near-kakinada-several-states-witnessing-heavy-rainfall/); about 100,000 people had been moved inland. It was the year’s first named storm in the North Indian Ocean, which usually has one by April or May. Bay of Bengal cyclones come in [two seasons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Indian_Ocean_tropical_cyclone), March to June and October to December, peaking in May and November, with very few from June to September. A cyclone needs water of at least about 26.5 °C through its top 50 metres, moist air, spin from Earth’s rotation and low wind shear, [NOAA explains](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/how-hurricanes-form.html); the summer monsoon blows hard near the sea and the other way high up, tipping a storm’s warm core over, so monsoon systems stay as depressions. When the monsoon turns, in May and in October, the shear drops while the sea is still warm, and the cyclones return.

slides.question: A tropical cyclone needs sea water of at least about how many degrees Celsius, down through its top 50 metres?
slides.explanation: About 26.5 °C, NOAA’s rule of thumb, warm enough to keep feeding the storm moist, rising air. The Bay of Bengal is that warm in summer too; what stops its summer cyclones is wind shear.

slides.alt: Animation on a deep-teal sea: a storm symbol spirals over a map of the Bay of Bengal to Kakinada, a bar chart of months shows two cyclone seasons peaking in May and November with a quiet monsoon gap, winds at two heights tilt a storm’s column, and Arnab’s week runs 24 to 29 October.

slides.prompt: Set the sea temperature, the wind shear and the latitude. Can you get a cyclone to form in the middle of the monsoon, with the sea still warm?
slides.takeaway: Warm water alone is not enough: with the monsoon’s strong shear the storm stays a depression. Cyclones need warm sea, low shear and distance from the equator together, which the Bay offers in spring and autumn.

slides.heading: Arnab’s week, by India’s weather office

events.text: A depression forms over the central Bay

slides.heading: Why the monsoon months are quiet
slides.text: From June to September the summer monsoon blows hard from the south-west near the sea and the opposite way high up. That difference, wind shear, tips a storm’s warm core over, so systems stay as depressions even over warm water. In May and in October the monsoon turns, the shear drops, and cyclones return.

slides.question: Why does the Bay of Bengal get so few cyclones from June to September, in the middle of the monsoon?
options: Strong wind shear tips storms over
The sea is too cold then
There is no rain to feed them
slides.explanation: The sea stays warm, but the monsoon’s winds change sharply with height. That shear tilts and tears a storm’s warm core, so monsoon systems stay as depressions; in May and October the shear drops.
